title: Justice Department cuts off evidence sharing with Minnesota investigators probing fatal ICE shootings | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Federal investigators in Minnesota abruptly stopped sharing evidence last month with state authorities investigating the fatal ICE shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

The move — which could hamper the state’s probe of the two killings by ICE agents — is the latest in a series of reversals that have frustrated Minnesota officials, with federal authorities repeatedly cooperating with state and local investigators before suddenly changing course and cutting off cooperation days, or even hours later.

Minnesota investigators said in court filings Tuesday thatsay the Justice Department still has not turned over key evidence to local authorities, including a statement by one of the officers who shot Pretti, a crucial piece of evidence as the Hennepin County attorney investigates the killing.

State investigators are also now blocked from accessing the cellphone of the agent who fatally shot Good, her clothing, the firearms used to shoot Pretti, the gun Pretti possessed, and other physical evidence from the scene of Pretti’s shooting, such as projectiles and shell casings, according to a sworn statement from Drew Evans, superintendent of Minnesota’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA.)

The state of Minnesota investigators are also seeking evidence in thenon-fatal shooting of Venezuelan immigrant Julio Sosa-Celis.The ICE officer, Christian Castro, faces state and federal charges related to the shooting and investigation.

Minnesota investigative authorities are still battling the Justice Department in federal court in Washington, DC, for access to the evidence needed to continue their investigations.

CNN has reached out to the Justice Department and the Minnesota US attorney’s office for comment.

The sudden change in DOJ’s posture came after a three-week period beginning in late June when the US attorney’s office for Minnesota and the BCA, the state’s lead investigative agency, negotiated an agreement to share evidence in the shootings.

According to the court records filed Tuesday, federal law enforcement provided evidence including Good’s vehicle, the gun used to shoot her, body-worn camera footage, officer statements, and other evidence. The Minnesota investigators also shared evidence its agents collected with federal agents.

The following month, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, thanked federal prosecutors at a press conference for the evidence sharing. At the time, Moriarty believed all the evidence in the cases had been shared with her office or would be soon.

Within days of the press conference, federal officials in Minnesota stopped cooperating with local authorities — and offered no explanation, the state said in their filings.

According to Tuesday’s filings, Moriarty’s team later discovered key evidence had not been shared.

Moriarty said in a sworn statement that she repeatedly reached out to Daniel Rosen, the US attorney for Minnesota, to resume evidence-sharing. Rosen told Moriarty several times his office was “pausing” cooperation but was “optimistic” that more information could be shared “soon.”

But, on September 10, Rosen informed Moriarty that his office would stop sharing evidence “indefinitely,” citing “challenges with D.C.”

Moriarty said in her statement that she “was left with the understanding” that federal authorities would not share any additional evidence with state and local investigators “unless and until there was a change in policy on that sharing coming out of Washington D.C.”

Moriarty acknowledged a notable distinction in the otherwise normal working relationship between federal and local law enforcement.

“Indeed, in all other matters including complex homicide cases, mass shootings, drug and gun cases, and many other types of cases, collaboration and information sharing with federal officials continues as normal,” Moriarty wrote. “The pause on information sharing is unique to these matters.”
